newsitem.title: CROATIA: Jews protest reburial of Croatian fascists.
newsitem.headline: Jews protest reburial of Croatian fascists.

text.p: Croatian officials said on Friday the remains of about 100 soldiers from Croatia's World War Two fascist army would be reburied alongside anti-Nazi Partisan fighters, prompting Jewish outrage.

Croatia's 1941-45 Nazi puppet Ustasha regime massacred many thousands of Jews and Serbs. In 1991, Croatia won independence from communist Yugoslavia under a nationalist government that has been accused of whitewashing the fascist past.

The parliamentary commission for the victims of the Second World War said the Ustasha soldiers would be reburied beside Croats who fought with the communist Partisan resistance at a site in the Adriatic seaside town of Omis on Sunday.
Members of Croatia's contemporary armed forces would take part in a memorial ceremony at Omis' Vrisovci cemetery, commission spokesman Florijan Boras told Reuters.

He said the reburial was requested by descendants of Ustasha soldiers who were long distressed that their loved ones had been dumped into unmarked mass graves near Omis by Yugoslav communist authorities at the end of World War Two.

"This is a private, family affair. The initiative did not come from the government. I hope it will not be unnecessarily politicised. It's our sacred duty to bury our perished in a dignified manner," Boras said.

"According to international conventions, all victims of war -- Ustasha included -- have a right to be buried properly, regardless of circumstances. The families of the Partisans, except three, I think, agreed to a joint burial."

The Simon Wiesenthal Centre, a prominent Jewish group that monitors respect for the victims of Nazism and investigates alleged Nazi war criminals who may still be living, strongly protested to the Croatian government over the Omis reburial.
In a statement issued by its office in Paris, the centre objected especially to what it said were plans by Croatian military officers to carry Ustasha coffins at the ceremony.
"This ... is an insult to the memory of those very victims for whom your (parliamentary) commission (for the victims of World War Two) was established," the centre said.
"Rather than reconciliation, this event transmits a perverse lesson to the young generation of a manifest continuity between Ustasha policy and today's forces of the Republic of Croatia."
Shimon Samuels, the Simon Wiesenthal Centre's European director, urged the Croatian parliament to withdraw its auspices over the ceremony and cancel the reburial.

President Franjo Tudjman stirred an uproar last April when he said he wanted to rebury the bones of Croatian fascists at a Yugoslav-built memorial to Jews and Serbs slain at the Ustasha's Jasenovac concentration camp.
Jewish protests forced him to shelve the proposal.
A leading state-run Croatian newspaper defended the Omis ceremony on Friday by emphasising Croats were not to be reburied beside Jews and Serbs as in Jasenovac.
"This is an event in which Croats are (symbolically) making peace among themselves," the daily Slobodna Dalmacija said.

But it added a note of doubt: "Some wonder whether this is the best way to make peace or whether this is political necrophilia and exhibitionism whose end result would be new political controversies and squabbles."
Slobodna Dalmacija said the Omis town government was paying for the reburial.
